Fix a defect in `scripts/logs`, which was added in the previous commit (`e80e647c`) on this branch.

## The defect

`scripts/logs:9` builds its compose command as a hardcoded `docker compose`:

```
compose="docker compose --project-directory /var/substrate --env-file /var/substrate/substrate.env -f /var/substrate/docker-compose.yml"
```

The substrate VM runs Container-Optimized OS, which does not have the compose plugin. The project's own bootstrap script says so explicitly and detects at runtime — see `packages/infrastructure/src/substrate-bootstrap-script.ts:91-94`:

```
// COS has neither the compose plugin nor the standalone binary - fall back to docker:cli.
if docker compose version >/dev/null 2>&1; then DC='docker compose';
elif command -v docker-compose >/dev/null 2>&1; then DC='docker-compose';
else DC='docker run --rm -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock -v /var/substrate:/var/substrate -v /var/substrate/.docker:/root/.docker docker:cli compose'; fi
```

So `just logs <service>` would fail on the real VM.

## Task

Make `scripts/logs` run the same three-way detection **on the remote host** before invoking compose, so it works wherever the bootstrap script works. The detection runs inside the SSH command, not locally — the local machine's docker has nothing to do with it.

The compose flags themselves are correct and must not change: `--project-directory /var/substrate --env-file /var/substrate/substrate.env -f /var/substrate/docker-compose.yml`, then `logs -f <service>`.

Mind the quoting: the remote command is a single string passed through `gcloud compute ssh ... -- -t`, and `$DC`/`$service` must expand at the right time — the detection variables must survive to the remote shell, while the service name must be substituted locally. Verify with `bash -n` and by echoing the constructed command to check it reads correctly before it is sent.

Keep the existing one-line "why" comment style. One line noting that COS lacks the compose plugin is enough — cite the same reason the bootstrap script gives, do not restate its whole logic.

## Scope fence

Touch **only** `scripts/logs`. Do not touch `justfile`, any other script in `scripts/`, or anything under `packages/`. In particular do not refactor the shared detection into a new helper script — `scripts/substrate-vm` exists for the VM lookup and that boundary is fine as it is.

## Acceptance

- `bash -n scripts/logs` passes.
- The constructed remote command, when echoed, contains the full three-way detection and the unchanged compose flags.
- `just --evaluate` still succeeds and `just logs` still takes one `service` argument.
- You cannot run `just logs` against the real VM here — no GCP credentials. Say so in your report.

Definitive answer: **no, you don't need to.**

`master@` holds `roles/owner` on `cyc-admin-scripts` as an explicit project IAM binding — not inherited from being a Workspace super-admin. Owner is a strict superset of every role in the plan's table, so binding `compute.admin`, `cloudsql.admin`, `dns.admin` and the rest to `master@` would add nothing but noise to the policy.

The live picture:

| Principal | Roles today |
| --- | --- |
| `master@` | `owner`, `compute.osLogin`, `iap.tunnelResourceAccessor`, `run.developer` |
| `ungood@` | `compute.osLogin`, `iap.tunnelResourceAccessor`, `run.developer` |

Three things follow, and one of them simplifies a later step:

1. **Your super-admin instinct was half right.** Workspace super-admin doesn't itself confer GCP IAM — but it *is* a recovery path: a super-admin can claim Organization Administrator at the org level and grant themselves project Owner. So `master@` has two independent ways back in, and the explicit deployer grant is a third that earns nothing.

2. **"Break-glass" should mean *don't remove* Owner, not *add* deployer roles.** #87's rollout-safety line — "keep the direct `user:master@` break-glass binding at all times" — reads as an instruction to add something. It's really an instruction to leave the existing Owner binding alone. The `bootstrap` project must use additive `gcp.projects.IAMMember`, never authoritative `IAMPolicy`, or an apply would silently strip Owner. That's worth stating explicitly since it's a one-word difference with a catastrophic failure mode.

3. **Step 11 gets simpler.** `master@`'s `osLogin`/`iap`/`run.developer` bindings come from the `deployers` list (`compute.ts:39`, `run-reports-job.ts:126`), so dropping per-user entries removes them — harmlessly, because Owner already covers all three. `master@` needs no group membership and no replacement grant.

input.prompt: Extract all concrete recommendations about super admin accounts: how many there should be, whether they should be used for daily work, separation between super admin and Organization Administrator roles, what each role can and cannot do, MFA/security key requirements, break-glass/recovery account practices, monitoring and alerting, and any specific guidance on separating Workspace super admin from GCP org admin. Be specific and quote the actual recommendations.

content.content:
# Super Admin Account Best Practices - Key Recommendations

## Account Separation
The document emphasizes keeping super admin accounts distinct from daily operations. It states: *"you should implement policies that will secure your super admin accounts and make users less likely to attempt to use them for day-to-day operations."*

Specifically, consider having separate login credentials: *"Give super admins a separate account that requires a separate login. For example, user alice@example.com could have a super admin account alice-admin@example.com."*

## Role Delegation
Rather than using super admin for routine tasks, the guidance recommends designating Organization Administrators. You should *"create a private Google Cloud administrator group in your Google Workspace or Cloud Identity super admin account"* and add Organization Administrators to this group—but notably, not the super admin user itself.

The Organization Administrator role has *"a smaller set of permissions that are designed to manage your day to day organization operations."*

## Security Requirements
Multi-factor authentication is mandatory: *"Enforce multi-factor authentication on your super admin accounts as well as all accounts that have elevated privileges."*

Additional hardening includes using *"a security key or other physical authentication device to enforce two-step verification"* and keeping *"the security key in a safe place, preferably at your physical location."*

## Monitoring
Set up automated alerts: *"set up alerts that will notify you when a SetIamPolicy() API call is made"* to detect unauthorized policy changes.

## Recovery Preparedness
Ensure *"Organization Administrators are familiar with the super admin account recovery process"* while keeping self-recovery disabled as a security best practice for new accounts.

input.prompt: Extract: what folders are and why they exist, the required IAM roles to create and manage folders (Folder Admin, Folder Creator, Folder Editor etc and their role IDs), how IAM inheritance works from organization to folder to project, typical folder hierarchy patterns and examples, limits on folder nesting depth, and how folders relate to organization policy and access control delegation.

content.content:
# Google Cloud Folders: Key Concepts and Management

## What Folders Are

Folders function as organizational nodes within Google Cloud's resource hierarchy. They enable grouping of projects and other folders to create structured, hierarchical organizations. As the documentation explains, "A folder can contain projects, other folders, or a combination of both."

## Purpose and Benefits

Folders serve several critical functions:
- **Resource organization** by department, environment, or application
- **Policy enforcement** at granular levels
- **Access control delegation** to specific teams
- **Cost management** across organizational units

The hierarchy allows operators to "group resources that share common allow or deny policies."

## Required IAM Roles

Key roles for folder management include:

| Role | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| **Folder Admin** (`roles/resourcemanager.folderAdmin`) | Create, edit, delete, move folders; manage IAM permissions |
| **Folder Creator** (`roles/resourcemanager.folderCreator`) | Create new folders |
| **Folder Editor** (`roles/resourcemanager.folderEditor`) | Edit folder properties |
| **Folder Viewer** (`roles/resourcemanager.folderViewer`) | View folder structure |

## Hierarchy Constraints

- Maximum nesting depth: **10 levels**
- Parent folder child limit: **300 direct child folders**
- Display names must be unique within the same hierarchy level
- Folder names: 3-30 characters, starting/ending with letters or digits

## Access Control Delegation

IAM policies cascade hierarchically. When you grant a role at the folder level, that permission applies to all contained projects, enabling efficient delegation without managing individual project permissions.

content.text:
Both docs read, and the live state makes this concrete. Here's what's actually there:

**Org-level IAM on `cyccommunitysailing.org` (`307534406562`)**

| Role | Member |
| --- | --- |
| `roles/owner` | `user:master@` |
| `roles/resourcemanager.organizationAdmin` | `user:master@` |
| `roles/iam.principalAccessBoundaryAdmin` | `user:master@` |
| `roles/resourcemanager.projectCreator` | **`domain:cyccommunitysailing.org`** |
| `roles/billing.creator` | **`domain:cyccommunitysailing.org`** |

Folders: one, `system-gsuite`, auto-created by Google. Projects sit flat under the org. `ungood@onetrue.name` holds **nothing** at org level.

## Three divergences from the guidance

**1. `master@` is the super admin *and* the Organization Administrator.** This is the specific thing the best-practices page tells you not to do. Its model is that super admin is a break-glass identity, and Organization Administrator — "a smaller set of permissions designed to manage your day to day organization operations" — is a *different* principal, held by a private group that pointedly *excludes* the super admin. Right now those are one account, so there's no separation to enforce.

**2. `master@` holds org-level `roles/owner`, which nothing needs.** `organizationAdmin` is the role Google designed for this. Owner at the org node is strictly more than that and is the single most dangerous binding you have.

**3. `projectCreator` and `billing.creator` are bound to `domain:`** — every Workspace member at CSC can create GCP projects and billing accounts. For a sailing nonprofit where staff have Workspace accounts, that's almost certainly unintended. It's also where most of those 12 junk `sys-*` projects came from.

## The model I'd recommend

| Tier | Who | Holds | Used for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Super admin | `master@`, `commander@` (#81) | Workspace super admin. **No org IAM roles.** | Break-glass only. Security keys, stored physically. |
| Org admin | a **domain** account, e.g. `jason@cyccommunitysailing.org` | `organizationAdmin` via a private group | Org policy, folders, org IAM, new projects |
| Deployer | `ungood@onetrue.name` via `it-admins@` | the `deployer` role from #87 | Daily work. Never touches org IAM. |

Removing org roles from `master@` is safe and reversible: a Workspace super admin can always re-grant itself `organizationAdmin`. That's exactly the recovery path the docs describe, and it's *why* the separation costs you nothing.

## The decision you actually have to make

**`ungood@onetrue.name` should not be the Organization Administrator**, and that's the part your question was circling.

It's external to the Workspace. You cannot enforce 2SV policy on it, you cannot suspend it during offboarding, and its password reset runs through `onetrue.name` — outside CSC's control entirely. That's tolerable for the *deployer* tier, where the blast radius is one project's resources and #87 is fencing it properly. It's not tolerable for a tier that can rewrite org IAM.

So: a domain account for the admin tier, ~$4.20/mo nonprofit rate. `ungood@onetrue.name` stays your working identity and gets deploy rights through `it-admins@` — which is precisely what #87 builds. Nothing in the current plan changes.

## Folders: not yet

The folders doc sells delegation and policy inheritance, and you'd get real value from both **if** you had per-environment or per-team projects. You don't — you have one real project plus cruft. #108 splits *Pulumi* projects, not GCP projects, so it doesn't create the need either.

The honest trigger to revisit: when you stand up a genuine `dev` project alongside `prod`, so `deployer` can be granted once at a folder rather than twice per project. Until then a folder tree is structure without a payload.

## What I'd do first

The cheapest high-value change isn't the account split — it's **narrowing those two `domain:` bindings to a group**. That's one `gcloud` command each, no new accounts, and it closes self-service project and billing creation for the whole staff.

Want me to file these? I'd suggest three issues: narrow the `domain:` bindings (P1, small), split super-admin from org-admin (P2, depends on #81 for `commander@`), and a note on #74 since this is the roles-as-IaC picture it asks for. None of it blocks #87 — I'd keep going on step 2 either way.

content.content:
# Domain-Restricted Sharing Constraint Analysis

## What It Blocks

The `iam.allowedPolicyMemberDomains` constraint prevents principals outside allowed domains from being granted IAM roles. When violated, operations fail with the error: "One or more users named in the policy do not belong to a permitted customer."

## Scope: New Bindings Only

This legacy managed constraint applies exclusively to **new IAM role assignments**. Existing bindings remain unaffected after policy enforcement.

## Customer ID Specification

Organizations must specify identifiers in the `allowed_values` list. Two formats are supported:

1. **Organization principal sets**: `principalSet://iam.googleapis.com/organizations/[ORG_ID]`
2. **Google Workspace customer IDs**: Retrieved via `gcloud organizations list` (appears as `DIRECTORY_CUSTOMER_ID`)

The documentation emphasizes: "Your organization principal set and Google Workspace ID are not automatically allowed."

## Scoping and Exceptions

The constraint supports conditional enforcement using resource tags but **does not permit exceptions for specific principals**. The documentation notes that the constraint "does not support denying values," limiting flexibility compared to custom organization policies.

## Outside Principals When Enabled

When enforced, principals from non-allowed domains are blocked entirely from receiving new role grants. The policy cannot be circumvented through standard UI or API operations.

content.text:
Both answerable precisely.

## 1. Limitations of an external Organization Administrator

**No IAM role is off-limits.** `organizationAdmin` works identically for an external principal — org IAM, folders, project creation, Pulumi, audit logs, `gcloud organizations list`. Nothing in the role degrades.

There are four real constraints, one of which matters a lot:

**Domain Restricted Sharing** (`constraints/iam.allowedPolicyMemberDomains`) is the one technical wall. Not enabled today — your Organization Policy API isn't even turned on, so nothing is enforced. If you ever enable it:

- It blocks **new** grants to outside principals. Existing bindings survive untouched.
- It has **no per-principal exception mechanism**. You can't allowlist just `ungood@onetrue.name`.
- The fix is adding `onetrue.name`'s customer ID to `allowed_values` — which then permits *any* `@onetrue.name` account. Since you run that Workspace, that's probably acceptable, but it's a domain-wide door, not a keyhole.

**The hard ceiling — and this is the one I'd want you to internalize:** GCP `organizationAdmin` gives you **zero Workspace capability**. Not user management, not group administration, not domain-wide delegation, and critically **not super-admin recovery**. An external account can never be a Workspace super admin — that requires a domain account, always.

So under your model, if `master@` is lost or locked out, `ungood@onetrue.name` can rebuild the entire GCP org and still cannot get back into Workspace. **This makes #81 (`commander@`) substantially more important, not less** — it becomes your only Workspace recovery path rather than a nice-to-have second pair of hands.

The other two are minor: Context-Aware Access device policies can't bind to an unmanaged identity, and your existing group-nesting limitation (`hasMember` resolves nesting in-domain only — the one you already hit with oauth2-proxy) means `it-admins@` must keep `ungood@` as a *direct* member, never nested.

## 2. Multiple organizations

**Yes, without qualification.** IAM is per-resource, and there is no exclusivity of any kind — one Google identity can hold `organizationAdmin` in as many GCP organizations as you like, simultaneously.

The distinction worth being clear on: `ungood@onetrue.name` being a *managed account* in the `onetrue.name` Workspace governs its **lifecycle** — you control it as that Workspace's admin. It does not give it a "home" GCP org or restrict which orgs may grant it roles. Those are orthogonal. Bind it to `cyccommunitysailing.org` and `gcloud organizations list` simply starts returning both.

Two practical notes:

- **Keep separate gcloud configurations per org.** You already run `CLOUDSDK_ACTIVE_CONFIG_NAME=isthmia` (`flake.nix:76`), and step 5 of the #87 plan makes that config project-local. That's exactly the right shape — it stops you from running a CYC command while pointed at the family org.
- **One credential now spans two organizations.** A compromise of that single account is a compromise of both. That's the substantive cost of the convenience, and it's the argument for the security key from the best-practices page — one physical key covering both blast radii is cheap.

## Where this leaves the model

You're actually satisfying the main structural recommendation. The docs' core ask is that super admin and Organization Administrator be **different principals** — and `master@` super admin + `ungood@onetrue.name` org admin is exactly that separation. content.text:
Verified, and the answer is cleaner than you might expect.

## `organizationAdmin` grants exactly zero deploy permissions

All 36 permissions are IAM-policy and hierarchy management. Of permissions touching `compute.`, `sql.`, `secretmanager.`, `run.`, `artifactregistry.`, or `dns.` — **zero**. It cannot create a VM, a secret, or a Cloud Run job. On its own it makes deployment no easier at all.

## But it does make the `bootstrap` project pointless

It includes `resourcemanager.projects.setIamPolicy`. So `ungood@` as org admin can **grant itself Owner on any project, at any time**.

That kills #87's entire rationale. The argument for splitting out `bootstrap` was:

> if `infrastructure` keeps creating project-level bindings, `deployer` needs `projectIamAdmin`, which lets it grant itself Owner — making the least-privilege claim cosmetic.

If `ungood@` is org admin, it can already self-escalate to Owner permanently and at will. The split would be guarding a door in a building with no walls. **Least privilege for a solo admin who is also the org admin is theater** — and I'd rather say that plainly than build an elaborate structure that only looks like security.

## So: yes, drop both. Here's the whole thing

Two bindings replace the entire IAM half of #87:

| Scope | Binding | Buys you |
| --- | --- | --- |
| org `307534406562` | `ungood@` → `roles/resourcemanager.organizationAdmin` | Administer org IAM without `master@` |
| project `cyc-admin-scripts` | `ungood@` → `roles/owner` | Deploy without `master@` |

No custom role. No `bootstrap` stack. No `StackReference`. No `pulumi import`. No `retainOnDelete` migration. No group-propagation waits. `config.ts:14` doesn't even change — Owner subsumes the `run.developer`/`osLogin`/`iap` grants it produces, and leaving that loop alone costs nothing.

**#87 goes from 11 steps to 5**, and every `master@` apply disappears.

## What survives — and it's the part that mattered

The entire tooling half. Look back at #87's evidence: 14 ADC expiries, 3 non-interactive reauth failures, wrong auth tables, module-scope `getClientConfig`, no preflight. **None of that was IAM.** The IAM gap forced the `master@` logins, but the tooling faults caused the actual misery, and they're untouched by this simplification.

Remaining: step 2 (`doctor`), step 3 (lazy `getClientConfig`), step 5 (project-local ADC + doc fixes), step 6 (promote the check).

## When the deployer role comes back

**#118, the GitHub Actions deploy.** A CI service account must *not* hold org admin — that identity genuinely needs a scoped role, and the self-escalation argument becomes real again because a service account isn't a person who can be trusted to behave. Build `deployer` then, bound to the WIF service account. Same for a second human developer, who should land in `it-admins@` rather than getting org admin.

That's not deferred work you'll regret — it's building it when there's finally something to protect against.

**One gap to know about:** `organizationAdmin` includes only *read* on org policy (`orgpolicy.policy.get`, `policies.list`, `constraints.list`). Setting policies needs `roles/orgpolicy.policyAdmin` separately. Narrowing those two `domain:` bindings works fine — that's `organizations.setIamPolicy`, which you'd have — but enabling Domain Restricted Sharing later would need the extra role.

content.text:
Now I can answer the mapping question concretely. The key structural fact first:

## Pulumi projects and GCP projects are not the same kind of thing

| Pulumi concept | What it is | GCP equivalent |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **project** (`bootstrap`, `infrastructure`, per-app) | code organization — which program owns which resources | **none** |
| **stack** (`prod`, `dev`) | an environment instance | **one GCP project** |
| — | isolation / quota / billing boundary | **GCP project** |
| — | IAM + policy delegation boundary | **GCP folder** |

Your repo already does the right thing: `gcp:project` is set per-stack in `Pulumi.prod.yaml`, and `config.ts:11` defaults non-prod stacks to `cyc-admin-scripts-dev`. **Stack → GCP project is already your mapping.** Don't change it.

**Do not make per-app GCP projects.** All your apps — portal, Directus, people-hub, FreeScout — share one substrate VM and one Cloud SQL instance. Separate GCP projects would force Shared VPC and cross-project service accounts to reassemble something you already have for free. import pathlib

p = pathlib.Path(
    "/Users/ungood/workspaces/personal/isthmia/.claude/worktrees/deployer-access"
    "/.claude/plans/deployer-access.md"
)
s = p.read_text()
n = 0


def sub(old, new):
    global s, n
    assert s.count(old) == 1, f"matched {s.count(old)} times:\n{old[:160]}"
    s = s.replace(old, new)
    n += 1


# --- Approach section 1: the role is for the CI identity, not a human group. ---
sub(
    """- A custom role `deployer` (`gcp.projects.IAMCustomRole`), plus a set of predefined roles, bound to
  `group:it-admins@cyccommunitysailing.org` only. See "Permissions" below.""",
    """- A custom role `deployer` (`gcp.projects.IAMCustomRole`), plus a set of predefined roles, bound to
  the `deploy-runner` service account. See "Permissions" below.
- The `deploy-runner` service account itself — the identity GitHub Actions will impersonate in #118.
  This project creates it and grants it; #118 adds the Workload Identity Federation pool, the
  binding from the GitHub repository principal, and the workflow.""",
)

# --- Who this is for. Replaces the group rationale with the CI rationale. ---
sub(
    """### 2. How `infrastructure` reads the identities""",
    """**Who the `deployer` role is for.** Not for you. `ungood@` holds `roles/owner` on the project
(see "Human access" below), which already covers everything `pulumi up` does. The scoped role exists
for `deploy-runner`, the identity a GitHub Actions run assumes. That is the principal that must not
be able to escalate: a workflow is repo-triggered code, so a compromised run holding
`resourcemanager.projects.setIamPolicy` could grant itself Owner and keep it. Scoping is real
security there in a way it would not be for a human who is already an organization admin.

A second human developer is out of scope. When one arrives, bind them to the same role set through
a group rather than granting Owner; nothing here has to change to allow that.

### Human access

Granted by `master@` in the console, not by Pulumi, and recorded in `docs/manual-setup.md`:

| Principal | Scope | Role |
| --------- | ------------------- | ------------------------------------------- |
| `ungood@onetrue.name` | organization `307534406562` | `roles/resourcemanager.organizationAdmin` |
| `ungood@onetrue.name` | project `cyc-admin-scripts` | `roles/owner` |

`organizationAdmin` grants no deploy permission at all — all 36 of its permissions are IAM-policy
and hierarchy management. Project `roles/owner` is what makes `pulumi up` work. The two are separate
grants serving separate purposes: administering the organization without `master@`, and deploying
without `master@`.

This is also why **no step in this plan needs a `master@` apply**. Project Owner covers creating the
custom role, the service accounts, and the project IAM bindings that `bootstrap` owns, so you apply
`bootstrap` yourself.

This repository uses a standard Github Pull Request flow. Direct pushes to the `main` branch are not allowed, instead
create changes in feature branches and submit a pull request to merge them to `main`. Pre-commit hooks will automatically
format and lint your changes. You can manually run checks with `just check` before committing.

## Authentication

Google Cloud access uses **two different credential types for two different purposes**. Don't confuse them.

| Purpose                                       | Credential                                | Recipe          | Underlying command                                                                    |
| --------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------- | --------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |

- Keep the three read-only lines `scripts/auth-status` already prints (active gcloud account, active configuration, active project) and its ADC-identity resolution via `print-access-token` + the tokeninfo endpoint. Read `scripts/auth-status` first — reuse its approach rather than reinventing it.
- Report **every** failure, not just the first. Run all checks, print all results, then exit non-zero if any failed.
- Print **one specific fix command** per failure. A check that says "ADC missing" without saying `just auth-adc` is worthless.
- Exit 0 when everything passes.

The checks, with the fix each prints:

| Check | Fix printed |
| --- | --- |
| `gcloud`, `pulumi`, `just`, `podman` on PATH | `direnv allow . && direnv exec . true` |

| ADC file present | `just auth-adc` |
| ADC token is live (tokeninfo resolves) | `just auth-adc` |
| ADC identity is a user, not `report-runner@` | `just auth-adc` |
| `gcloud projects describe cyc-admin-scripts` succeeds | ask `master@` for project `roles/owner` |
| `pulumi whoami` succeeds | `pulumi login` |
| `scripts/podman-docker-host` exits 0 | `podman machine start` |

**Important — the ADC-identity check is a WARNING at this step, not a failure.** `just auth-adc` still impersonates `report-runner@` today; step 5 is what changes that. - Replace the `auth-status` recipe with `doctor`, in the same `[group('auth')]`.

- Follow the justfile conventions established in the previous commit and visible in the file: exactly one line of doc comment per recipe, a body of one or two lines, `[group(...)]` on every recipe. **Docs:** `README.md` has a "Checking your auth state" section (around line 66) documenting `just auth-status`. Update it for `doctor` — say that it checks and prints fixes, not merely reports. Keep it short and match the surrounding prose style.

Touch only: `scripts/doctor` (new), `scripts/auth-status` (delete), `justfile`, and the `README.md` section about checking auth state.

Do **not**:
- Change `just auth-adc`'s `--impersonate-service-account` flag. That is step 5.
- Change the credential tables at `README.md:48` or in `CLAUDE.md`. Those are wrong (they claim pulumi and docker use the `gcloud auth login` session when they actually use ADC) but fixing them is step 5, bundled with the change that makes the corrected text true.
- Touch anything under `packages/`, `.envrc`, or `flake.nix`.
- Add `just deploy-bootstrap` — that is step 4.

## Acceptance

- `just doctor` runs, prints a readable report, and exits 0 in a healthy environment.
- With a deliberately broken input (e.g. `CLOUDSDK_CORE_ACCOUNT` unset or PATH missing a tool), it reports that specific failure with its fix and exits non-zero — and still reports the other checks rather than stopping at the first.

- `scripts/auth-status` no longer exists and nothing references it (grep for it).

Fix a reproducibility gap in the devshell. Small, self-contained change.

## The problem

Three command-line tools are used by scripts in `scripts/` but are not declared in the devshell's package list in `flake.nix` (the list runs from roughly `flake.nix:62` — `just`, `nodejs_22`, `corepack_22`, `gam`, `pulumi`, `pulumiPackages.pulumi-nodejs`, `google-cloud-sdk`, `rumdl`, `entire`, and the treefmt wrapper):

- **`jq`** — used by `scripts/doctor:29` to parse the tokeninfo response. On this machine it resolves to `/etc/profiles/per-user/ungood/bin/jq`, which is the developer's personal nix-darwin profile, not the devshell.
- **`curl`** — used by `scripts/doctor:29`. Resolves to `/usr/bin/curl` (macOS system).
- **`nc`** — used by `scripts/pulumi-tunnel:26` in the tunnel wait loop. Resolves to `/usr/bin/nc` (macOS system).

CLAUDE.md states the flake exists to give a reproducible development environment. These three break that: on a fresh clone, another developer's machine, or a GitHub Actions runner (which issue #118 will add), `jq` is simply absent. `scripts/doctor` then produces an empty identity and reports "ADC token does not resolve to an identity (tokeninfo lookup failed)" with the fix `just auth-adc` — a misleading diagnosis. Because `just doctor` is now a dependency of `just deploy` and `just preview`, that wrong diagnosis blocks deploys.

## Task

1. **Add the three tools to the devshell package list in `flake.nix`.** Keep the list's existing formatting and ordering style. Pick the right nixpkgs attribute for netcat and confirm it actually provides an `nc` binary on darwin — do not guess; verify by entering the shell and running `command -v nc`.

2. **Extend the PATH check in `scripts/doctor`** (currently `for tool in gcloud pulumi just podman` at line 34) to also cover `jq`, `curl`, and `nc`, so a missing one is reported as itself with the `direnv` fix, rather than surfacing later as a confusing downstream failure.

## Verification — this is the important part

Changing `flake.nix` means the devshell must be rebuilt. You must confirm the shell still evaluates and that all three tools resolve **inside the devshell, from the nix store** rather than from the ambient system:

- Rebuild/enter the shell (`direnv exec . true`, or `nix develop -c true`). This may take a few minutes; that is expected.
- Inside the devshell, verify `command -v jq`, `command -v curl`, and `command -v nc` each resolve to a `/nix/store/...` path. If `curl` still resolves to `/usr/bin/curl`, say so in your report rather than forcing it — a system curl is acceptable if declaring it causes problems, but you must report which way it ended up.
- Run `just doctor` and confirm it still exits 0 and prints a resolved ADC identity.
- Run `just ci`.

## Scope fence

Touch only `flake.nix` and `scripts/doctor`. Do not touch `flake.lock` beyond whatever the rebuild does on its own — do **not** run `nix flake update`. Do not touch the justfile, other scripts, `packages/`, or docs.

If adding `curl` to the devshell causes any TLS or certificate problem on macOS, drop `curl` from the package list, keep `jq` and netcat, and explain the decision in your report. That is an acceptable outcome — a system `curl` is present on every platform this runs on, whereas `jq` genuinely is not.

## Acceptance

- All three tools are available in the devshell, with their resolved paths reported.
- `just doctor` exits 0 and reports a real ADC identity.
- `just ci` passes.

## Task

Two calls to `gcp.organizations.getClientConfig({})` run at **module scope**, so an expired credential kills the entire Pulumi program before it can produce a diff — with an `oauth2:` error that never says "re-authenticate". Issue #87 recorded this happening 14 times across two deploy sessions. Make both lazy so an expired token fails one resource, with that resource named.

**Site 1 — `packages/infrastructure/src/substrate.ts:52`:**

```ts
const registryToken = gcp.organizations.getClientConfig({}).then((config) => config.accessToken);
```

Used at the `registries[0].password` of the `substrate-image` `docker.Image` (around line 62-67).

**Site 2 — `packages/infrastructure/src/run-reports-job.ts:42`:**

```ts
const registryToken = gcp.organizations.getClientConfig({}).then((config) => config.accessToken);
```

Used at the `registries[0].password` of the `report-runner-image` `docker.Image` (around line 50-57).

In both cases, replace the module-scope `const` with an inline `gcp.organizations.getClientConfigOutput({}).accessToken` at the `password` field. `getClientConfigOutput` returns a Pulumi `Output`, which `password` accepts as an `Input<string>`, and it is resolved during resource registration rather than at module load.

Remove the now-unused `registryToken` constants. In `run-reports-job.ts` check whether `registryAddress` (line 41) is still worth keeping as a separate constant or should be inlined too — match whatever reads better against the surrounding code; do not churn it if it is used more than once.

## Context you cannot derive

- Both sites carry an existing comment explaining *why* an OAuth2 access token is used rather than a docker credential helper (podman's auth config lives elsewhere). Keep that reasoning. The repo's comment rule is that comments explain why, in a line or two — do not expand these into an explanation of the laziness change, and do not delete them.
- `substrate.ts:49` says "Auth mirrors run-reports-job.ts". Keep the two sites structurally parallel so that statement stays true.
- Both `docker.Image` resources have `dependsOn: artifactRepositoryAccess`. Do not change that.

## Scope fence

Touch only `packages/infrastructure/src/substrate.ts` and `packages/infrastructure/src/run-reports-job.ts`, and within them only the token plumbing described above. Do not change image tags, contexts, platforms, push settings, the Cloud Run job, or any IAM. Do not move service accounts or project IAM — those are steps 7 through 9.

- `just ci` passes (this includes the TypeScript build, which is the main correctness signal — `getClientConfigOutput` must typecheck against the `password` field).
- `pulumi preview` would show **no diff**: this is a pure refactor of how the token is obtained, not a change to any resource's inputs. You almost certainly cannot run `pulumi preview` here (it needs live GCP credentials and a podman machine) — say so in your report rather than guessing at the result.

# Manual setup steps

Most of this platform is infrastructure-as-code (Pulumi, in `packages/infrastructure`). A handful of
steps **cannot** be — they live in Google consoles, the Workspace Admin console, or the domain
registrar, or they involve secret _values_ that must never enter git. This doc is the running record
of every such out-of-band step, so setting up a fresh environment (or recovering one) doesn't rely
on memory.

Legend: `[ ]` = to do for a new setup, `[x]` = done for the current production setup (as of this doc).

> Why these can't be code: OAuth "Web application" clients and the **External** consent screen have
> no Terraform/Pulumi resource; domain-wide delegation and Workspace settings live in the Admin
> console and would require super-admin credentials that our access policy deliberately keeps out of
> automation (see [CLAUDE.md](../CLAUDE.md) → Access policy); registrar delegation is at the domain
> registrar; and external credentials (OAuth secrets, third-party logins) are set out of band by
> design — Pulumi declares only the container for those. Internal keys/passwords with no meaningful
> human choice are the exception: Pulumi generates and manages those values directly (see §3).

---

## 1. Project & organization bootstrap (super-admin)

Done as a Workspace **super-admin** (`master@cyccommunitysailing.org`). Reserved to super-admins per
the access policy — not day-to-day deploy identities.

- [x] GCP project `cyc-admin-scripts` created under the org.
- [x] Org policy / project-root IAM as needed.
- [ ] Any Google API that must be enabled by hand (most are enabled in code via the `enableService`
      helper; enable by hand only if a chicken-and-egg case appears).

## 2. Per-person deploy/dev access

Each contributor authenticates locally; nothing is stored in the repo. See
[README.md → Authentication](../README.md#authentication).

- [ ] `just auth-gcp` — `gcloud auth login` as your own account (e.g. `ungood@onetrue.name`), which is
      granted deploy + impersonation rights in `packages/infrastructure/src/config.ts`.
- [ ] `just auth-adc` — ADC impersonating `report-runner@…` for running tools locally.
- Do **not** log in as a super-admin for development.

## 3. Secret values (Secret Manager)

Most secrets here are **external credentials** — Pulumi declares only the container, and the value
is added out of band and never committed:

I'm working out the gcloud commands the user needs to run as master@ to grant the two roles—one at the org level assigning organizationAdmin, and I'm noting they're likely already on the right account to execute it.

There's a caveat worth flagging though: granting roles/owner on a project to someone outside the organization can trigger Google's owner-invitation flow, where the binding doesn't take effect until the invited user accepts an emailed invitation, so I should mention that requirement.

I'll add `--condition=None` to the gcloud commands to sidestep any interactive prompts on newer versions.

I shouldn't run these commands myself since granting IAM ownership externally is an outward-facing, hard-to-reverse action — I'll give the user the commands (confirming they're authenticated as master@ first) along with verification steps and the invitation caveat, and mention they can use the `!` prefix to run them directly in-session.

content.text:
Here you go. Run these as `master@` — which is already your active account, so no switch needed.

**Verify who you are first:**

```sh
gcloud config get-value account   # expect master@cyccommunitysailing.org
```

**1. Organization Administrator on the org:**

```sh
gcloud organizations add-iam-policy-binding 307534406562 \
  --member="user:ungood@onetrue.name" \
  --role="roles/resourcemanager.organizationAdmin" \
  --condition=None
```

**2. Owner on the project:**

```sh
gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding cyc-admin-scripts \
  --member="user:ungood@onetrue.name" \
  --role="roles/owner" \
  --condition=None
```

**Verify both landed:**

```sh
gcloud organizations get-iam-policy 307534406562 \
  --flatten="bindings[].members" \
  --filter="bindings.members:ungood@onetrue.name" \
  --format="value(bindings.role)"

gcloud projects get-iam-policy cyc-admin-scripts \
  --flatten="bindings[].members" \
  --filter="bindings.members:ungood@onetrue.name" \
  --format="value(bindings.role)"
```

You should see `organizationAdmin` from the first and `owner` plus the three existing roles from the second.

**One thing to watch.** `ungood@onetrue.name` is outside `cyccommunitysailing.org`, and Google treats granting project **Owner** to an external user differently from other roles — it can send an invitation email to that address that must be accepted before the binding takes effect. If the second command succeeds but `get-iam-policy` doesn't show `owner`, check that inbox rather than re-running it. The org-level grant has no such flow.

`--condition=None` just suppresses the interactive condition prompt in recent gcloud.

If you'd rather these run right here so the output lands in the conversation, prefix with `!` — e.g. `! gcloud projects get-iam-policy cyc-admin-scripts ...`. I've deliberately not run the grants myself; they're outward-facing IAM changes and yours to make.

# Isthmia Bootstrap

A second Pulumi project that owns identity and access for the `cyc-admin-scripts` GCP project: the
`deploy-runner` service account CI impersonates to deploy, and the project-level IAM bound to it.

resource-scoped.

and `substrate-bootstrap-script.ts` in `packages/infrastructure`, which build the platform VM's
cloud-init.

just deploy-bootstrap

for role in \

  roles/iap.tunnelResourceAccessor roles/cloudsql.admin roles/servicenetworking.networksAdmin \
  roles/dns.admin roles/artifactregistry.admin roles/secretmanager.admin \
  roles/run.developer roles/cloudscheduler.admin \
  roles/iam.serviceAccountAdmin roles/iam.roleAdmin roles/resourcemanager.projectIamAdmin

done
```

#!/usr/bin/env bash

use flake

# Shared by every worktree of this repo, so a new session worktree doesn't need its own
# `just auth-gcp`. Isolates these credentials from the developer's personal gcloud config,
# not worktrees from each other.
export CLOUDSDK_CONFIG="$(git rev-parse --git-common-dir)/../.gcloud"
mkdir -p "$CLOUDSDK_CONFIG"

# google-auth-library (and the Go provider behind @pulumi/gcp) hardcode
# $HOME/.config/gcloud for ADC and never look at CLOUDSDK_CONFIG, so this must be set
# separately or Node tools and Pulumi keep reading the old, unshared location.
export GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS="$CLOUDSDK_CONFIG/application_default_credentials.json"=== auth-adc ===
# Point Application Default Credentials at your own gcloud login
[group('auth')]
auth-adc:
    gcloud auth application-default login

---
#### Access policy (least privilege)

Root-level control of the GCP project and Google Workspace is reserved for the two Workspace
super-admin accounts, `master@cyccommunitysailing.org` and `commander@cyccommunitysailing.org`
(only `master@` exists today; `commander@` is planned as a second break-glass admin so root access
is never held by a single account). Those accounts are the only ones used for **configuration**
changes — org policy, project-root IAM, enabling services by hand, Workspace settings.

Individuals (e.g. `ungood@onetrue.name`) are granted only the narrower rights they need to test and
deploy: deploy permissions plus the ability to **impersonate service accounts** (never to log in as,
or hold the credentials of, the super-admin accounts). Day-to-day development and deploys therefore
run as your own account impersonating a service account — not as an admin. New principals default to
no access; grants are added deliberately in `packages/infrastructure/src/config.ts`.

#### Google Cloud (Sheets, Calendar, deploys)

base = pathlib.Path(
    "/Users/ungood/workspaces/personal/isthmia/.claude/worktrees/deployer-access"
)
n = 0


def sub(path, old, new):
    global n
    p = base / path
    s = p.read_text()
    assert s.count(old) == 1, f"{path}: matched {s.count(old)} times:\n{old[:160]}"
    p.write_text(s.replace(old, new))
    n += 1


# 1. manual-setup §7 — the Owner command cannot work via CLI. State it as fact.
sub(
    "docs/manual-setup.md",
    """Run both as `master@` (check with `gcloud config get-value account` first):

```sh
gcloud organizations add-iam-policy-binding 307534406562 \\
  --member="user:ungood@onetrue.name" \\
  --role="roles/resourcemanager.organizationAdmin" \\
  --condition=None

gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding cyc-admin-scripts \\
  --member="user:ungood@onetrue.name" \\
  --role="roles/owner" \\
  --condition=None
```""",
    """The organization grant runs as `master@` from the CLI (check with
`gcloud config get-value account` first):

```sh
gcloud organizations add-iam-policy-binding 307534406562 \\
  --member="user:ungood@onetrue.name" \\
  --role="roles/resourcemanager.organizationAdmin" \\
  --condition=None
```

**The project Owner grant cannot be made from the CLI.** `ungood@onetrue.name` is outside
`cyccommunitysailing.org`, and Google refuses `roles/owner` for an external principal over the API:

```text
ERROR: (gcloud.projects.add-iam-policy-binding) INVALID_ARGUMENT
  type: ORG_MUST_INVITE_EXTERNAL_OWNERS
```

It must go through the console, which sends an invitation the recipient accepts:

1. <https://console.cloud.google.com/iam-admin/iam?project=cyc-admin-scripts>
2. **Grant access** → New principals: `ungood@onetrue.name`
3. Role: **Basic → Owner** → **Save**
4. Accept the invitation emailed to `ungood@onetrue.name`. The binding appears only afterwards.

Every other role grants to an external principal over the CLI normally — only `roles/owner` is
restricted this way. If you would rather avoid an external Owner, the alternative is to grant the
eleven predefined roles from the design doc's "Permissions" table plus
`roles/iam.serviceAccountAdmin`, `roles/iam.roleAdmin`, and `roles/resourcemanager.projectIamAdmin`
(the last three are what applying `packages/bootstrap` needs and the scoped `deployer` role
deliberately withholds). That is Owner-equivalent in practice, since `projectIamAdmin` can grant
itself anything.""",
)

# 2. manual-setup §7 — the verification block's stale lead-in.
sub(
    "docs/manual-setup.md",
    """Verify each landed:""",
    """Verify each landed (the Owner binding only after the invitation is accepted):""",
)

# 3. manual-setup §7 — the caveat is now stated above as fact, so drop the tentative note.
sub(
    "docs/manual-setup.md",
    """> `ungood@onetrue.name` is outside `cyccommunitysailing.org`, and Google treats granting project
> **Owner** to an external user differently from other roles: it can send an invitation email that
> must be accepted before the binding takes effect. If the command succeeds but `get-iam-policy`
> does not list `owner`, check that inbox rather than re-running it. The organization-level grant
> has no such flow.

""",
    "",
)

# 4. CLAUDE.md access policy — impersonation is no longer how deploys run.
sub(
    "CLAUDE.md",
    """Individuals (e.g. `ungood@onetrue.name`) are granted only the narrower rights they need to test and
deploy: deploy permissions plus the ability to **impersonate service accounts** (never to log in as,
or hold the credentials of, the super-admin accounts). Day-to-day development and deploys therefore
run as your own account impersonating a service account — not as an admin. New principals default to
no access; grants are added deliberately in `packages/infrastructure/src/config.ts`.""",
    """Individuals (e.g. `ungood@onetrue.name`) hold project-level rights and never the credentials of a
super-admin account. Day-to-day development and deploys run as **your own account**: `gcloud auth
login` and ADC are both you, and project `roles/owner` is what makes `pulumi up` work. See
[docs/manual-setup.md](docs/manual-setup.md) §7 for how that is granted, and why
`organizationAdmin` — which confers no deploy permission at all — is a separate grant.

The scoped `deployer` role in `packages/bootstrap` is not for people. It belongs to `deploy-runner`,
the service account GitHub Actions assumes (#118). A repo-triggered workflow is the principal that
must not be able to grant itself Owner; a human who is already an organization admin cannot
meaningfully be constrained by one.""",
)

print(f"{n} edits applied")
